t: Super Ugly Number — Multi-Pointer Merge of Prime Multiples
o: We must build the sorted sequence of numbers whose prime factors all come from `primes`, and return the nth one (1-indexed, starting with 1). This generalizes the classic 'Ugly Number II' problem: instead of primes {2,3,5} we have up to 100 arbitrary primes. In Example 1, each next number is the smallest value of the form (an earlier ugly number) × (a prime): after 1 we get min(2,7,13,19)=2, then 4=2·2, then 7, then 8=2·4, etc. Since n can be 10^5 with 100 primes, a naive approach that checks every integer for membership would be far too slow; we need to generate candidates in order rather than test them.
k: Every super ugly number > 1 equals an earlier one multiplied by some prime in the list.
Keep one pointer per prime into the generated sequence; the next number is the minimum over primes[p_i] * ugly[i].
Advance every pointer whose product ties for the minimum to avoid duplicates.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force with a heap
a.i: Generate candidates by repeatedly popping the smallest ugly number from a min-heap and pushing its products with every prime. A set prevents duplicates. This directly mirrors the definition but does O(n·m) heap pushes, which is acceptable yet wasteful compared to the pointer method.
s: Push 1 into a min-heap and an empty seen-set containing 1.
Pop the smallest value n−1 times; each time push val*p for every prime p if not already seen.
The value popped on the nth pop is the answer.
a.t: O(n · m · log(n·m)) where m = primes.length — each of n pops pushes m values into the heap.
a.sp: O(n · m) — the heap and seen set can hold up to n·m candidates.

a.n: Approach 2: Dynamic programming with per-prime pointers (optimal)
a.i: Maintain the sorted array `ugly` of results built so far. For each prime keep an index pointing at the smallest ugly number whose product with that prime hasn't been emitted yet. The next ugly number is simply the minimum of these m candidate products — no heap needed since there are only m candidates. Advancing all pointers achieving the minimum skips duplicates in O(m) time.
s: Initialize ugly[0] = 1 and idx[i] = 0 for every prime.
For k from 1 to n−1: compute cand[i] = ugly[idx[i]] * primes[i] for all i.
Increment idx[i] for every i with cand[i] == ugly[k] (handles duplicates like 2·7 = 7·2).
a.t: O(n · m) — for each of n slots we scan m candidate products twice (min + duplicate advance). With n ≤ 10^5 and m ≤ 100 this is ~10^7 operations.
a.sp: O(n + m) — the result array plus one index per prime.

w: In an interview, mention the heap idea briefly, then implement the DP-with-pointers solution — it is simpler, faster, and uses less memory. Key pitfalls: forgetting to advance **all** pointers tied at the minimum (produces duplicates), using 32-bit intermediates (products can overflow before fitting the final answer — use long/64-bit math), and off-by-one indexing since the sequence starts at ugly[0]=1. Edge cases: n=1 returns 1 regardless of primes; a single prime just yields powers of it. Follow-ups: how to speed up when m is huge (use a heap of (product, prime, pointer) triples for O((n+m) log m)), or handle unsorted/duplicated primes (dedupe first, sorting isn't required for correctness of the pointer method).
